mainTopic: A search through several verses for the source that all Torah food prohibitions also forbid benefit (איסור הנאה), with each proposed source challenged in turn.
overview: The גמרא is searching for the Torah source that anything forbidden to eat is also forbidden for benefit (איסור הנאה). Each attempt uses the same method: find words in a verse that are not needed for their own case, move them to all prohibitions, and then move them from eating to benefit. Each time, the גמרא adds that the verse's burning rule does not carry over to all forbidden items. The first attempt uses 'לא תאכל' in the verse about an outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside. It is challenged because that verse is needed for רבי שמעון's teaching about where disqualified offerings are burned. The reply is that רבי יונתן learned the rule from the leftover מילואים meat instead. But that verse is needed for רבי אלעזר's general לאו on eating disqualified holy items. אביי then returns to the first verse and says 'לא תאכל' there is extra because of רבי אלעזר. רב פפא rejects this, since a general לאו brings no lashes, and offers a new source: 'לא יאכל' about impure sacred meat, which is already forbidden by a קל וחומר and a הקש from מעשר. The amud ends with רבינא suggesting that those words only add a second לאו, citing אביי's rulings on eating a פוטיתא and an ant. The answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The extra words teach a ban on benefit
steps.stepSummary: The derivation reaches its end: since eating is already forbidden, the extra phrase is redirected to teach איסור הנאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is not needed to teach about eating, apply it to teach the prohibition of benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a derivation from the previous lines. An extra phrase in the Torah, not needed to forbid eating, is used to forbid getting any benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method is 'אם אינו ענין': if a phrase teaches nothing new in its own place, we move it to a new subject. Eating these items is already forbidden, so the phrase must be teaching something more. That something is that one may not benefit from them at all.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not relevant (to its own topic): the method of moving an extra phrase to a new topic
Apply it to the topic of
The prohibition against deriving any benefit
Eating

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the general rule, according to this view, that anything forbidden to eat is also forbidden for benefit.

phrases.english: And if it is not relevant to eating,
phrases.notes: Eating was already forbidden elsewhere, so the phrase is extra here.

phrases.english: apply it to the prohibition of benefit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לַאֲכִילָה, תְּנֵהוּ עִנְיָן לְאִיסּוּר הֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the derivation begun on the previous amud.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All Torah food prohibitions also carry איסור הנאה.

steps.title: Must every forbidden item then be burned?
steps.stepSummary: If all prohibitions are learned from the חטאת, perhaps they should all be destroyed by burning, as the חטאת is.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then perhaps: just as here the disposal is by burning, so too all the prohibitions in the Torah must be disposed of by burning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with the comparison it just made. If we learn from the חטאת, maybe we should copy its burning too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When one law is learned from another, we might think every detail carries over. The חטאת must be burned. The worry is that this would require burning every forbidden food, such as חמץ or כלאי הכרם.

keyTerms.meaning: If so / perhaps (introducing a possible wrong conclusion)
Just as here ... so too (a comparison formula)
Burning
The prohibitions in the Torah

phrases.english: If so, just as here it is by burning,
so too all prohibitions in the Torah are by burning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the comparison in Step 1 extends.
steps.kashyaTarget: The learning of all prohibitions from the חטאת verse
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the comparison is complete, the burning requirement should also carry over to all prohibitions.

steps.title: Only sacred things need burning
steps.stepSummary: The word 'בקדש' limits the burning requirement to sacred items. Other prohibitions do not need burning.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'In the sacred place ... it shall be burned in fire.' Things of the sacred are burned, but not all the prohibitions in the Torah are burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry using the word 'בקדש' in the verse. Only sacred items must be burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison carries over איסור הנאה, but not the burning. The word 'בקדש' ties the burning to holy items only. Ordinary forbidden foods share the ban on benefit, but not the way they are destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: In the sacred (place), or regarding sacred things
It shall be burned in fire

phrases.english: The verse says: 'In the sacred ... shall be burned in fire,'
sacred items are by burning,
but not all prohibitions in the Torah are by burning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every forbidden item must be burned like the חטאת.
steps.terutzMaskana: Burning applies only to sacred items, while איסור הנאה applies to all prohibitions.

steps.title: That verse is already needed for another teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that 'בקדש באש תשרף' cannot be used to limit burning, because it is needed for רבי שמעון's teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: And did this verse, 'In the sacred ... shall be burned in fire,' come for this purpose? It is needed for the teaching of רבי שמעון!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge begins. The verse just used in Step 3 already has a different job, so it cannot also teach this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A verse that is fully used for one teaching is not normally available for a second one. If 'בקדש' teaches where offerings are burned, it cannot also limit burning to sacred items. This challenge threatens the entire derivation from the חטאת verse.

keyTerms.meaning: Did it come for this purpose?
It is needed (for another teaching)
For the teaching of רבי שמעון

phrases.english: And this verse, 'In the sacred ... shall be burned in fire,'
did it come for this purpose?!
It is needed for the teaching of רבי שמעון!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַאי ״בַּקֹּדֶשׁ ... בָּאֵשׁ תִּשָּׂרֵף״ לְהָכִי הוּא דַּאֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the verse used in Step 3's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using 'בקדש באש תשרף' to limit burning to sacred items
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse is already used up by רבי שמעון's teaching about the place of burning.

steps.title: רבי שמעון's teaching about where offerings are burned
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי שמעון uses the verse to teach that a disqualified חטאת, and other disqualified holy items, are burned in the sacred place.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי שמעון says: 'In the sacred ... shall be burned in fire' teaches that a חטאת is burned in the sacred place. I would only know this about the חטאת. How do we know that disqualified offerings of קדשי קדשים and the altar portions of קדשים קלים are also burned there? The verse says: '(And every) ... in the sacred ... shall be burned in fire.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא that proves the challenge of Step 4. It shows exactly what job the verse already does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, 'בקדש' tells us WHERE to burn: inside the Temple area. He then widens it from the חטאת to other disqualified holy items. Since the verse is fully used for this, it is not free for the limitation in Step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: A sin-offering
Disqualified offerings of the most holy level
The parts placed on the altar from offerings of lesser holiness
From where do we know?

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'בקדש' means the PLACE of burning (inside the Temple). In Step 3 it was read as limiting burning to sacred ITEMS. The challenge depends on noticing this difference.

phrases.english: As it was taught: רבי שמעון says:
'In the sacred ... shall be burned in fire' —

phrases.aramaic: לִימֵּד עַל חַטָּאת שֶׁשּׂוֹרְפִין אוֹתָהּ בַּקֹּדֶשׁ.
phrases.english: this teaches that a חטאת is burned in the sacred place.
I would only know this case alone;
disqualified offerings of the most holy level
and altar portions of lesser offerings: from where do we know?
The verse teaches: '(And every) ... in the sacred ... shall be burned in fire.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source behind the challenge in Step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That the verse is already used for another teaching

steps.title: רבי יונתן used a different verse
steps.stepSummary: The reply: רבי יונתן learned the rule from the verse about leftover מילואים meat, where 'לא יאכל' is extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: רבי יונתן, your teacher, said it from this verse: 'And if any of the מילואים meat or the bread is left until morning, etc.' There was no need to say 'it shall not be eaten.' So why does the verse say it? If it is not needed for its own case, because it already says 'you shall burn the leftover in fire,' apply it to the other prohibitions in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is answered by switching to a new verse, about the leftover meat of the מילואים offerings. There, the words 'לא יאכל' are extra and can be redirected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah already commands that the leftover be burned, which obviously means it may not be eaten. So 'לא יאכל' adds nothing to its own case and is moved to all other prohibitions. This verse is not needed for רבי שמעון's teaching, so the challenge falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Your teacher
The meat of the inauguration offerings of the משכן
There was no need for the verse to say
For its own case
Leftover sacrificial meat past its time

phrases.english: He said to him: רבי יונתן, your teacher,
said it from this verse:
'And if any of the meat of the מילואים is left over,'
'or of the bread, until the morning, etc.'
for there was no need to say 'it shall not be eaten,'
so why does the verse say 'it shall not be eaten'?
If it is not relevant to its own case,
since it is already written 'you shall burn the leftover in fire,'
apply it to the other prohibitions in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן רַבָּךְ מֵהַאי קְרָא קָאָמַר לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 4 and 5 by replacing the source verse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule rests on the חטאת verse (the source cited by רבי יהושע בן לוי), which is already needed for רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule comes from 'לא יאכל' in the מילואים verse, which is free to be redirected.

steps.title: The new verse also teaches a ban on benefit
steps.stepSummary: Using the מילואים verse, the same final step is repeated: since eating is already forbidden, the phrase teaches איסור הנאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is not needed to teach about eating, apply it to teach the prohibition of benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the same closing line as Step 1, but now it rests on the new verse. This completes רבי יונתן's derivation on solid ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating forbidden foods is already prohibited elsewhere, so 'לא יאכל' moves one step further, to benefit. The conclusion stays the same: all forbidden foods are also forbidden for benefit. Only the source has changed.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יונתן, anything the Torah forbids to eat is also forbidden for benefit. His source is the extra 'לא יאכל' in the verse about leftover מילואים meat, not the חטאת verse, which רבי שמעון needs for the place of burning. Step 9 will challenge this source too.

phrases.english: And if it is not relevant to eating,
apply it to the prohibition of benefit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לַאֲכִילָה, תְּנֵהוּ עִנְיָן לְאִיסּוּר הֲנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the derivation from the new verse in Step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רבי יונתן, all Torah food prohibitions include איסור הנאה, learned from 'לא יאכל' in שמות כט:לד. This source is challenged in Step 9.

steps.title: Burning is limited to leftover sacred meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא prevents a wrong conclusion. Just because נותר must be burned, we should not think that every forbidden item must be burned. The verse 'ושרפת את הנותר' limits burning to נותר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Lest you say: just as here the item is burned, so too all Torah prohibitions must be burned! The verse says 'You shall burn the leftover'. The leftover is burned, but the other Torah prohibitions are not burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the מילואים derivation from step 7. It blocks the idea that every forbidden item needs burning, because the verse says only נותר is burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 learned איסור הנאה for all prohibitions from the מילואים verse. Someone might then copy the burning rule too. The word 'הנותר' tells us only leftover sacred meat is burned. Other prohibitions are forbidden in benefit, but they have no burning requirement.

keyTerms.meaning: Sacrificial meat left over past the time it may be eaten
Burning, the required way of disposing of certain items
All the prohibitions in the Torah

phrases.english: Lest you say: just as here it is with burning,
so too all prohibitions in the Torah are with burning!
The verse says: 'You shall burn the leftover'
Leftover meat is with burning,
but all the prohibitions in the Torah are not with burning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the מילואים derivation by repeating the burning limitation, as step 3 did for the first verse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every forbidden item would need burning, like נותר.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only נותר is burned. Other prohibitions only carry איסור הנאה.

steps.title: The מילואים verse is needed for רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges using 'לא יאכל' in the מילואים verse to teach איסור הנאה. Those words are needed for רבי אלעזר's teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: And did this 'it shall not be eaten' come for this purpose? It is needed for the teaching of רבי אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the derivation from steps 6-7. It says 'לא יאכל' is not extra at all, because רבי אלעזר uses it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole derivation depended on 'לא יאכל' being an extra phrase. If רבי אלעזר needs it for his own law, it is not free to teach איסור הנאה. This is the same kind of objection as step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: Did it come for this purpose?
It is needed for something else
It shall not be eaten (the מילואים verse)

phrases.english: And this 'it shall not be eaten'
did it come for this?
This is needed for the teaching of Rabbi Elazar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source given in steps 6-8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'לא יאכל' in the מילואים verse is extra
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A phrase used for another law cannot be treated as extra and used to teach איסור הנאה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: a לא תעשה for eating disqualified holy items
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר learns from 'לא יאכל כי קדש הוא' that eating anything disqualified in the קדש carries a negative commandment.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי אלעזר said: 'It shall not be eaten, for it is holy' teaches about anything disqualified in the holy place. The verse comes to put a לא תעשה on eating it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי אלעזר to show the קשיא is real. The phrase is already in use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר reads the מילואים verse as a general rule for all פסולי המוקדשין: whoever eats them breaks a לא תעשה. Because the phrase teaches this, it is not extra for a benefit prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: Disqualified, such as a sacrifice that became invalid
A negative commandment, punishable by lashes
Holy; here, the sacred place or sacred items

steps.whyThisMatters: רבי אלעזר's general rule sets up אביי's answer. Once it exists, the 'לא תאכל' in the first verse becomes extra.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Elazar said:
'It shall not be eaten, for it is holy'
anything in the holy that is disqualified,

phrases.aramaic: בָּא הַכָּתוּב לִיתֵּן לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה עַל אֲכִילָתוֹ.
phrases.english: the verse comes to place a negative commandment on eating it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the קשיא in step 9.
steps.raayaObject: That 'לא יאכל' in the מילואים verse is already used

steps.title: אביי returns to the first verse and reverses the reading
steps.stepSummary: אביי goes back to the verse of the outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside. Since רבי אלעזר already forbids eating it, 'לא תאכל' there is extra. It teaches that all Torah prohibitions are forbidden in benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Really, use the first verse, but reverse it. Let the verse write only 'it shall be burned in fire', and it would not need 'it shall not be eaten'. Why does the verse say 'it shall not be eaten'? It is not needed for its own case, which we know from רבי אלעזר. So apply it to all Torah prohibitions. And it is not needed for eating, so apply it to איסור הנאה.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the קשיא. He drops the מילואים verse and finds the extra phrase in the first verse, about an outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the first verse was rejected because 'בקדש באש תשרף' was needed for רבי שמעון. אביי 'reverses' it: the extra part is 'לא תאכל', not the burning phrase. רבי אלעזר's rule already forbids eating a disqualified חטאת. So 'לא תאכל' moves to all prohibitions, and then from eating to benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually; it introduces a return to an earlier position
The first verse (ויקרא ו:כג, an outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside)
Reverse it
Why does the verse need to say this?
If it is not needed for its own subject, apply it elsewhere
A prohibition against benefiting from an item

steps.confusionAlert: 'Reverse' does not mean reading the verse backwards. It means switching which phrase counts as extra: 'לא תאכל' instead of the burning phrase.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Actually, the first verse, and reverse it:
Let it write 'it shall be burned in fire',
and it would not need 'it shall not be eaten'.
Why does the verse say 'it shall not be eaten'?
If it is not needed for its own matter,
since that is derived from Rabbi Elazar,
apply it to all prohibitions in the Torah.
And if it is not needed for eating,
apply it to the prohibition of benefit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לְעוֹלָם מִקְרָא קַמָּא, וְאֵיפוֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of steps 9-10 by returning to the first verse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first verse failed because its burning phrase is needed for רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'לא תאכל' in the חטאת verse is extra because of רבי אלעזר. It teaches איסור הנאה for all Torah prohibitions.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is אביי's source for the general rule that Torah food prohibitions also forbid benefit. רב פפא challenges it in Step 13 and offers a different verse.

steps.title: Again, burning applies only to נותר
steps.stepSummary: Using אביי's source, the גמרא again limits burning to leftover sacred meat. Other prohibitions are only forbidden in benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Lest you say: just as here it is burned, so too all Torah prohibitions are burned. The verse says 'the leftover'. The leftover is burned, but the other Torah prohibitions are not burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes אביי's derivation by repeating the burning limitation, as it did for the earlier sources.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's source is a verse that also says 'באש תשרף', so one might think every prohibition must be burned. The word 'הנותר' limits burning to leftover holy meat. Things like חמץ בפסח or שור הנסקל are forbidden in benefit but need no burning.

keyTerms.meaning: Lest you say, introducing a possible mistaken conclusion
Leavened bread on Pesach, an example of a general prohibition
An ox sentenced to stoning, another example

steps.whatToRemember: By אביי's reversal, 'לא תאכל' in the verse of the outer חטאת whose blood was brought inside is extra because רבי אלעזר already forbids eating disqualified holy items. So all Torah prohibitions carry איסור הנאה, but only נותר requires burning. The next step shows רב פפא disputing this source.

phrases.english: Lest you say: just as here it is with burning,
so too all prohibitions in the Torah are with burning.
The verse says 'the leftover'
the leftover is with burning,
but all the prohibitions in the Torah are not with burning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's derivation with the burning limitation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to אביי, all Torah prohibitions carry איסור הנאה, learned from the extra 'לא תאכל'. Burning is limited to נותר.

steps.title: רב פפא says אביי's extra words are needed for lashes
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא argues that 'לא תאכל' by the outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside is not extra. It is needed to give that prohibition its own specific לאו, so that one gets מלקות for it. רבי אלעזר's general לאו does not bring מלקות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: Maybe those words come to give this case its own specific negative commandment. If we only had רבי אלעזר's source, nobody would get lashes, because we do not give lashes for a general negative commandment.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא attacks אביי's proof. He says the words 'לא תאכל' are not extra after all, because they do a real job of their own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said 'לא תאכל' was extra because רבי אלעזר already forbids eating an outer חטאת whose blood was brought inside. רב פפא answers that רבי אלעזר's verse is a לאו שבכללות, one broad לאו covering many disqualified offerings, and such a לאו does not bring מלקות. So the Torah needs 'לא תאכל' to make a specific לאו with lashes, and nothing is left over to teach איסור הנאה.

keyTerms.meaning: To give it its own specific negative commandment
For the case itself (not for a different teaching)
We give lashes (מלקות)
A general negative commandment that covers many different things at once

steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא agrees that eating an outer חטאת whose blood was brought inside is forbidden even under רבי אלעזר. His point is only that a general לאו brings no lashes, so the extra words are needed for punishment and are not truly 'extra'.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
But say it comes to designate a specific negative commandment
for the case itself it comes,
phrases.notes: The words 'לא תאכל' teach about that חטאת itself, an outer חטאת whose blood was brought inside.

phrases.english: for if it were only from Rabbi Elazar's source —
one does not receive lashes for a general negative commandment.
phrases.notes: רבי אלעזר's לאו covers all disqualified קדשים, so it is a 'general' לאו.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי: וְאֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's claim in Step 11 that 'לא תאכל' is extra.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's derivation of איסור הנאה from the extra 'לא תאכל' by the outer חטאת whose blood was improperly brought inside.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words are not extra. רבי אלעזר's general לאו brings no lashes, so the Torah needs a specific לאו for this case.

steps.title: רב פפא brings a new source from impure sacred meat
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rejects אביי's source and offers his own: 'לא יאכל' in the verse about sacred meat that touched something impure. He claims these words are unnecessary and asks what they come to teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב פפא said: we learn it from here. 'And the meat that touches anything impure shall not be eaten; it shall be burned in fire.' The verse did not need to say 'it shall not be eaten,' so why does it say it?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a new verse as the source for איסור הנאה. He points out that 'לא יאכל' seems unneeded, which sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse is about קדשים that became impure. רב פפא says 'לא יאכל' is extra, and extra words in the Torah must teach something new. He has not yet proven that they are extra; the next step does that.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (we drop the previous approach)
From here (introducing a new source)
Ritually impure
Why does the verse need to say this? (signals extra words)

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Pappa said: from here:
"And the meat that touches anything impure
shall not be eaten; it shall be burned in fire,"
for the verse did not need to say "it shall not be eaten,"
so why does the verse say "it shall not be eaten"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting אביי's source in Step 13, רב פפא offers a replacement source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The extra 'לא יאכל' said about impure sacred meat is the source for איסור הנאה.

steps.title: Why the words are extra: a קל וחומר from מעשר
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא proves 'לא יאכל' is extra. The ban on eating impure קדשים already comes from a קל וחומר: if lighter מעשר שני may not be consumed in טומאה, then stricter sacred meat surely may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the words are not needed for their own case, it is because that case is learned by a קל וחומר from the lighter מעשר. The Torah said about light מעשר, 'I did not consume any of it while impure.' Then holy meat, which is stricter, surely may not be eaten while impure!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows why 'לא יאכל' is not needed for its plain meaning. The rule already comes from logic, a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the וידוי מעשרות a person declares that he did not consume מעשר שני in טומאה, so מעשר may not be eaten that way. קדשים are holier than מעשר, so the same rule applies to them even more. Since logic already teaches this, 'לא יאכל' is left free to teach something else, איסור הנאה.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not needed for its own subject (so apply it to another teaching)
Logical argument: if the lighter case has a rule, the stricter case surely does
Tithe (here מעשר שני, holy but less holy than קדשים)
'I did not consume any of it while impure' (from the tithe declaration)
Sacred meat of offerings

phrases.english: If it is not needed for its own subject,
since that is derived by a kal vachomer
from the lighter tithe:
just as about the lighter tithe the Torah said
"I did not consume any of it while impure" —
phrases.notes: דברים כו:יד, from the tithe declaration.

phrases.aramaic: בְּשַׂר קֹדֶשׁ חָמוּר לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן?!
phrases.english: then stricter sacred meat, all the more so?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לְגוּפוֹ, דְּהָא נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִקַּל וָחוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in Step 14: why 'לא יאכל' is unnecessary.
steps.raayaObject: That 'לא יאכל' in ויקרא ז:יט is extra and free to teach איסור הנאה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from מעשר שני ('לא בערתי ממנו בטמא') to the stricter בשר קודש.

steps.title: Objection that logic cannot create a prohibition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a possible objection. A קל וחומר cannot create a לאו, so 'לא יאכל' would still be needed for its own case.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: 'We do not create a warning (a לאו) from logic.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up a possible problem with רב פפא's proof. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that a לאו cannot be learned from a קל וחומר alone. If so, the ban on eating impure קדשים would need the verse 'לא יאכל' after all, and רב פפא's proof would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (introduces a possible objection)
We do not derive a prohibition from logic alone

phrases.english: And if you will say
"We do not derive a warning from logical inference."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא אֵין מַזְהִירִין מִן הַדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the קל וחומר used in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ban on eating impure קדשים comes from the קל וחומר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A לאו cannot come from logic, so 'לא יאכל' is still needed for its own case and is not extra.

steps.title: The rule also comes from a verse that groups מעשר with offerings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ban does not rest on logic alone. It also comes from a הקש: one verse lists מעשר together with בכור and other קדשים, so the rules of מעשר carry over to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a comparison from the verse, as it is written: 'You may not eat within your gates the tithe of your grain, your wine, and your oil, or the firstborn of your cattle, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection. The ban on eating impure קדשים comes from a הקש, which counts as a real Torah source and not just logic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הקש compares two things that the Torah mentions together in one verse. Since this verse groups מעשר with בכור and other offerings, the טומאה ban on מעשר applies to קדשים as well. So the rule still has a source without 'לא יאכל', and those words stay free to teach איסור הנאה. Step 18 then puts the freed words to that use.

keyTerms.meaning: A הקש: an analogy from two things placed side by side in a verse
Within your gates (outside ירושלים)
Firstborn animals (a type of קדשים)
Etc. (the verse continues)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not dropping the קל וחומר. It adds the הקש so the rule does not rest on logic alone.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a הקש counts as a real Torah source that can support a prohibition, while a קל וחומר alone cannot.

phrases.english: It is a juxtaposition, as it is written:
"You may not eat within your gates
the tithe of your grain, your wine, and your oil
or the firstborn of your cattle, etc." —
phrases.notes: דברים יב:יז. מעשר and קדשים appear together in one verse, which makes the comparison.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Provides an alternate, stronger source (a הקש) that is not subject to the rule against learning a לאו from logic.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban on impure קדשים rests only on a קל וחומר, which cannot create a לאו.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban also comes from a הקש between מעשר and קדשים, so 'לא יאכל' remains extra.

steps.title: The extra words teach a ban on benefit from all forbidden things
steps.stepSummary: Since 'לא יאכל' is not needed for its own case, רב פפא applies it to all Torah prohibitions, and to the ban on benefit (הנאה), not just eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why does the verse say 'it shall not be eaten'? If it is not needed for its own subject, apply it to all the prohibitions in the Torah. And if it is not needed for eating, apply it to benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא finishes his proof. He shows what the extra words 'לא יאכל' really teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 15-17 showed that impure sacred meat is already forbidden through the הקש with מעשר. So the words are free for a new lesson. Using the rule 'אם אינו ענין', they are moved first to all Torah prohibitions, and then from eating to benefit. The result is that benefit is forbidden from all forbidden foods.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the verse need to say this?
If it is not needed for its own subject
Apply it to a different subject
Benefit, any use other than eating

steps.whatToRemember: For רב פפא, the ban on benefit from forbidden foods comes from the extra 'לא יאכל' in the verse about impure sacred meat.
steps.confusionAlert: 'לא יאכל' literally means 'shall not be eaten', yet here it ends up teaching a ban on benefit. That is because the words are extra for eating, so they are moved to a new subject.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is רב פפא's full answer to the main question of the sugya: where does the Torah forbid benefit from forbidden foods?

phrases.english: What does the verse teach by saying 'it shall not be eaten'?
If it is not needed for its own subject,
phrases.notes: Impure sacred meat is already forbidden through the הקש with מעשר.

phrases.english: apply it to all the prohibitions in the Torah.
And if it is not needed for eating,
phrases.notes: Eating these things is already forbidden by other verses.

phrases.english: apply it to benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the words are shown to be extra (Step 17), רב פפא uses them for a new lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Benefit from all Torah-forbidden items is banned, learned from the extra 'לא יאכל'.

steps.title: Must every forbidden item also be burned?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a problem. If all prohibitions are learned from this verse, maybe they must all be burned too, like the impure sacred meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, just as here the meat is burned, all prohibitions in the Torah should be burned too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the comparison it just made. It asks whether the verse's burning rule also carries over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same verse that says 'לא יאכל' also says the meat must be burned. If we copy the verse onto all prohibitions, it seems we should copy the burning rule too. That would mean every forbidden food must be destroyed by fire.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, or 'but then'; introduces a problem
Burning

phrases.english: But then: just as here it is by burning,
phrases.notes: The impure sacred meat must be burned.

phrases.english: so too all prohibitions in the Torah should be by burning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It tests whether the comparison in Step 18 goes too far.
steps.kashyaTarget: Applying the verse to all Torah prohibitions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the verse is applied to all prohibitions, its burning requirement should apply to them as well.

steps.title: The word 'הנותר' limits burning to sacred meat
steps.stepSummary: The verse says 'הנותר'. This limits burning to sacrificial meat, so other forbidden items do not need to be burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'the leftover'. The leftover sacred meat must be burned, but not all the prohibitions in the Torah must be burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 19 using a word in the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'הנותר' shows that burning is a special rule for sacrificial meat. So only the ban on benefit carries over to all prohibitions. The burning rule stays with קדשים.

keyTerms.meaning: The leftover sacrificial meat

phrases.english: The verse says 'the leftover':
the leftover sacred meat is burned,
but all the prohibitions in the Torah are not burned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the burning objection from Step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every forbidden item would have to be burned.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only sacrificial meat ('הנותר') is burned. The ban on benefit still carries over to all prohibitions.

steps.title: Maybe the extra words only add a second לאו
steps.stepSummary: רבינא suggests that 'לא יאכל' may not teach a ban on benefit at all. Perhaps it only adds a second לאו for eating impure sacred meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: But say instead that the words make a person break two לאוין for it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges רב פפא's whole derivation with a different reading of the extra words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא assumed that extra words must teach a new subject. רבינא says they could stay on the same subject and simply add a second לאו. Then one who eats impure sacred meat would get two sets of מלקות. If so, we have no source for a ban on benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead; offers another reading
To break two negative commandments by one act

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
But say it comes to make one break two prohibitions for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְאֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It reopens רב פפא's conclusion with another way to use the extra words.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's use of 'לא יאכל' for a ban on benefit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Extra words can add another לאו on the same act, so they need not move to a new subject.

steps.title: אביי shows that one act can bring many sets of מלקות
steps.stepSummary: רבינא supports his idea with אביי's ruling. Eating a small water creature brings four sets of מלקות, and eating an ant brings five.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't אביי say: If one ate a פוטיתא, he gets four sets of lashes. An ant: he gets five.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא brings a precedent from אביי to show that the Torah does repeat לאוין on a single act.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי counts several verses that each forbid eating creeping creatures. Each one adds its own set of מלקות. So repeating a לאו just to add punishment is normal. That makes רבינא's reading of 'לא יאכל' believable.

keyTerms.meaning: A small water creature
He receives מלקות (lashes)
An ant
Didn't he say? Introduces a supporting source

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'לָאו' is the word 'didn't', not a negative commandment.
steps.whyThisMatters: If רבינא's reading stands, רב פפא loses his source for the ban on benefit. The גמרא's answer comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: Didn't Abaye say:
If one ate a small water creature, he is flogged four times.
An ant: he is flogged five times.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבינא's suggestion in Step 21 with a precedent.
steps.raayaObject: That extra words can simply add another לאו for the same act
steps.raayaSupportSource: אביי: eating a פוטיתא brings four sets of מלקות, and eating an ant brings five
